data.title: <![CDATA[Treasury Proposes Rules Adding Biotechnology to Outbound Investment Security Program]]>
data.description:
The U.S. Department of the Treasury issued a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) to update the Outbound Investment Security Program (OISP) under direction from Congress in the Comprehensive Outbound Investment Security (COINS) Act, passed as part of the fiscal year 2026 National Defense Authorization Act.

Among the proposed changes, the Secretary of the Treasury is adding biotechnology to the list of technology sectors subject to the program, extending national security review into a space with direct implications for pharmaceutical dealmaking.

What does the proposed rule cover?

The COINS Act directs the Treasury Secretary to issue regulations requiring U.S. persons to notify Treasury of certain transactions involving covered foreign persons engaged in “notifiable technologies,” and to prohibit U.S. persons from engaging in other transactions involving covered foreign persons engaged in “prohibited technologies.”1,2

data.title: <![CDATA[Every AI Agent Will Eventually Fail: Why Healthcare Leaders Need Supervision, Not Hope]]>
data.description:
AI agents are moving into healthcare faster than most organizations can supervise them. In this conversation, Amy Brown, CEO of Authenticx, argues that every AI agent will eventually fail—and that the real differentiator isn't which company deploys AI first, but which one can see, catch, and correct what its AI is doing before a patient or member is harmed.

Learning Objectives:

  1. Learn why “every AI agent will fail” isn't a scare tactic—it's the reality of deploying probabilistic systems in high-stakes healthcare conversations.
  2. Understand what “supervision” actually means, and why it's different from dashboards, spot-checks, or a one-time launch checklist.
  3. Learn how healthcare leaders can build the continuous oversight needed to catch problems early—before they become patient safety or compliance risks.

data.title: <![CDATA[Roundup: Gilead Acquires Oral IL-23R Inhibitor From PepStar for $1.275 Billion, Zymeworks Licenses DLL3-Targeting T Cell Engager to Roche]]>
data.description:
Gilead Sciences, Inc. has entered a definitive agreement to acquire an oral IL-23R inhibitor program, including lead asset HCXT-2001, from PepStar Therapeutics Limited.

Gilead is set to pay $1.275 billion in upfront cash consideration, subject to customary adjustments, payable at closing. The transaction is expected to close in the fourth quarter of 2026 and is projected to reduce Gilead’s GAAP and non-GAAP EPS by approximately $0.79 to $0.83 in that quarter.1

HCXT-2001 is an investigational, clinical-stage, oral, macrocyclic peptide inhibitor of IL-23R with an extended half-life, currently in Phase I clinical trials, offering what Gilead describes as a potentially differentiated approach to oral IL-23 pathway inhibition.1 IL-23R is a clinically validated target in immune-mediated inflammatory diseases, including inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), with potential applications in psoriasis. The deal gives Gilead worldwide rights to the program and adds to the company’s inflammation and immunology portfolio, where it is building depth across multiple mechanisms and modalities.1

<![CDATA[MFN Is an Offer Pharma Can’t Refuse]]>
data.description:
President Trump’s Most-Favored Nation (MFN) initiative continues to impact the industry. Most recently, the deadline passed for mid-sized pharma and biotech companies to make deals with the administration or face serious tariffs on imported goods.

The deal is designed to both reduce prices that Americans pay for pharmaceuticals while also promoting an increase in domestic manufacturing. Since it was first announced, experts in the industry have spoken both in favor and against the deal. While the initial wave of deals focused on major pharma companies who can easily adjust strategies, launch new manufacturing projects, and absorb costs, the latest headlines focused on mid-sized pharma companies, who are less likely to be able to absorb new costs.

Pharmaceutical Executive spoke with John Stanford, executive director at Incubate, about the current status of MFN and how its impacting the industry. He focused not just on the unique impact on mid-sized pharmas, but also how these deals may force companies to adjust plans for future launches or drug research.

Pharmaceutical Executive: What are the unique considerations for MFN deals with mid-sized pharma companies?
John Stanford: The first thing to remember is that “mid-sized company” is a broad definition, so I want to be careful not to paint with too broad a brush. But mid-sized pharmaceutical companies are constrained in two ways that iconic manufacturers — a Pfizer, a Merck — are not.

The first constraint is that they simply have fewer products on the market. To the extent we saw details from the initial deals with large manufacturers, those agreements applied to specific products. When you have 30 or 40 products on the market, you have more margin to give on specific products, and you can tailor deals to what is most advantageous to you while still ceding some ground to the administration. But when you only have one or three products, you cannot absorb a 20 to 30 percent margin hit in the same way.

That brings us to the second constraint: capital. Something large companies have — in this industry and others — is access to substantial, low-cost capital. Mid-sized biopharmaceutical companies do not necessarily have that luxury. They may need all of their revenue to fund what comes next in their portfolio and pipeline, and they do not have the same access to Wall Street and public markets to tap into alternative sources of capital.

data.title: <![CDATA[Roundup: Alcon Acquires Neurotech and Encelto, Ai Proteins Enters Research Collaboration and License Agreement with Astellas Pharma ]]>
data.description:
Alcon has acquired Neurotech Pharmaceuticals, Inc., a company developing cell therapies for chronic and neurodegenerative eye diseases, for $550 million, with additional contingent payments possible upon achievement of commercial milestones.

The acquisition brings Encelto (revakinagene taroretcel-lwey), the first and only U.S. FDA-approved treatment for adults with idiopathic macular telangiectasia type 2 (MacTel), a rare, progressive retinal disease that causes irreversible central vision loss and has historically had no approved treatment options.1

Encelto is an encapsulated cell therapy intended for surgical intravitreal implantation that continuously releases recombinant human ciliary neurotrophic factor, a protein that helps protect retinal cells and reduce the loss of light-sensing photoreceptors.1 The FDA granted the therapy priority review and orphan drug designation and approved it under a biologics license application back in March 2025. The treatment is currently available only in the U.S.

“Neurotech’s innovative platform sits at the intersection of cell therapy, pharmaceuticals, and surgery, making it a highly complementary addition to our current capabilities and advancing our vision for the future of retinal disease treatment,” says David Endicott, chief executive officer of Alcon. “By combining Neurotech’s groundbreaking science and established commercial footprint with Alcon’s global reach and clinical expertise, we can help bring this innovation to more patients whose vision is threatened by MacTel.”

data.title: <![CDATA[FDA Grants Ultomiris Accelerated Approval in the U.S. for Adults with Primary Immunoglobulin A Nephropathy ]]>
data.description:
Alexion, AstraZeneca Rare Disease’s Ultomiris (ravulizumab) has been approved in the U.S. to reduce proteinuria in adults with primary immunoglobulin A nephropathy (IgAN) at risk for disease progression.

The approval follows by the FDA and is based on positive results from a pre-specified interim analysis of the I can Phase III trial, in which Ultomiris demonstrated a 43.4% reduction in proteinuria versus placebo at 34 weeks.1,2

What are the terms of the approval?

The indication is approved under accelerated approval based on reduction of proteinuria; it has not been established whether Ultomiris slows kidney function decline in patients with IgAN. Continued approval may be contingent on verification of clinical benefit in the ongoing I can Phase III trial, which is assessing the primary endpoint of change from baseline in estimated glomerular filtration rate at week 106, with data intended to support traditional FDA approval.1

Ultomiris is administered intravenously every eight weeks in adults, dosed by body weight, following a loading dose. Regulatory submissions based on the interim results are also under review in Japan and additional countries.1

data.title: <![CDATA[Median Drug Launch Prices Hit $257,000 as Access Barriers Persist, ICER and West Health Report Finds]]>
data.description:
The Institute for Clinical and Economic Review (ICER) and West Health released a new Launch Price and Access Report finding that median drug launch prices continue to exceed $250,000 per year, contributing to rising overall healthcare costs.

The report, which focused on net price ,which is the actual amount paid after rebates and discounts rather than the publicly listed price, found the median net launch price rose 35%, from $190,000 in 2022 to $257,000 in 2025, adjusted for inflation.1

What else did the report show?


While the median net launch price dipped by 2% between 2024 and 2025, it remained at historically high levels, with about one in four drugs introduced in 2025 carrying an annual net price exceeding $500,000, and an additional 34% launched between $200,000 and $500,000.1,2 Among newly approved drugs previously reviewed by ICER, only about one in three were priced at or below the organization’s recommended value-based benchmark, with the remainder exceeding their estimated value.2
